chapter.title: Pick one destination

cards.body: Ask a speaker 30 seconds before they stand up what their point is. Watch the pause. A talk is a walk you lead, and **a walk needs one destination**: if you can't name the place you're taking people, they'll follow you politely for 3 minutes and arrive nowhere.
cards.simpler: Ask a speaker, 30 seconds before they stand up, what their point is. Watch them pause. Think of a talk as a walk you lead. **A walk needs one destination.** If you can't name the place you're taking people, they will follow you politely for three minutes and end up nowhere.

cards.prompt: Sam has 3 minutes to speak at Jo's birthday dinner. Which of these is a destination, a place the listeners can actually arrive at?

options.text: Jo and the ten years we've known her
Jo shows up when it's inconvenient, and that's why we're all here.
Some funny stories, a bit about her job, then a toast

whyNot.a: That's the topic, not the point: it names the field you'll wander in, not the place you'll arrive.
whyNot.c: That's a list of stops, not a destination: three things to do, and no one sentence they add up to.

cards.reteach: A destination is one sentence someone could repeat on the way home. A topic is just the field you're standing in. A list is the route. Only the sentence tells you where the walk ends.

cards.title: Why one, not three
cards.body:
You'd think more points means more value. It's the reverse. Listeners can't rewind you, so **everything they keep has to fit in one hand**, and one sentence is about what a hand holds.

A point is a claim or an ask: something a person could agree with, argue with, or go and do. A *topic* is the subject area; a *point* is what you're saying about it. 'Sleep' is a topic. 'Go to bed 30 minutes earlier this week' is a point.

Every story, number and slide then has one job: carry people a step closer to that sentence. Anything that doesn't, you leave at home.
cards.simpler:
More isn't better here. Listeners can't rewind you, so **everything they keep has to fit in one hand**, and a hand holds about one sentence.

A point is a claim or an ask: something people could agree with, argue with, or do. A topic is only the subject. 'Sleep' is a topic. 'Go to bed 30 minutes earlier this week' is a point.

Every story and slide has one job: carry people closer to that sentence, or stay home.

cards.title: Priya's three tries
cards.body: Priya has 3 minutes at Monday's team meeting to introduce the new expense form. Her first destination is 'Expenses', a topic you could wander in for a week. Her second is 'the new form, why we changed it, and how to use it', which is three stops and no arrival. Third try, said out loud in 6 seconds: 'File each expense the day you spend it, and you'll be paid within the week.' Fifteen words, **one place to arrive**. She looks at her 11 slides and deletes 9 of them.
cards.simpler: Priya has 3 minutes at Monday's meeting to introduce a new expense form. Her first try is 'Expenses', a topic you could wander in for a week. Her second is 'the new form, why we changed it, and how to use it', which is three stops and no arrival. Her third, said out loud in 6 seconds: 'File each expense the day you spend it, and you'll be paid within the week.' Fifteen words, **one place to arrive**. She deletes 9 of her 11 slides.

cards.prompt: Dev has 3 minutes at his running club to talk about a new route. Which sentence should he write on his card before anything else?

options.text: The canal path: distance, lighting, safety, and where to park.
Run the canal path on winter evenings, because it's flat and lit until 11pm.
First I'll describe the path, then the lighting, then take questions.

whyNot.a: That's the topic broken into headings, not the point: nobody could agree or disagree with it.
whyNot.c: That's the running order, not the destination: it says what Dev will do, not where listeners end up.

cards.reteach: Test a sentence by asking: could someone nod or shake their head at it? A heading can't be argued with. A running order can't either. Only a claim or an ask can, and that's your destination.

cards.title: Write it before anything else
cards.body:
Write the sentence first, before notes, slides or jokes. Keep it to **15 words or fewer, with a verb**, because a verb is what turns a subject into something that happens. Count on your fingers if you have to.

Then say it out loud and time it. Under 10 seconds means it's small enough to carry. If it takes 20, you've got two destinations wearing one coat: split them and keep the one you'd save if the fire alarm went off.

Last test: could a listener text it to a friend afterwards without looking anything up? If yes, you've picked a place. If no, keep carving.
cards.simpler:
Write the sentence first, before notes, slides or jokes. Keep it to **15 words or fewer, with a verb**, because a verb turns a subject into something that happens.

Say it out loud and time it. Under 10 seconds means it's small enough to carry. Twenty seconds means two destinations wearing one coat: split them and keep the one you'd save in a fire.

Could a listener text it to a friend without looking anything up? If not, keep carving.

cards.body: Marcus was asked to speak for 3 minutes at his dad's retirement do. On his card he wrote 'Dad's career'. He spoke for 9 minutes, covered 4 jobs and 2 countries, and finished with 'so, yeah'. Spot it early: **if your sentence has no verb, it's a topic**, and a topic has no end, so neither will you.
cards.simpler: Marcus was asked to speak for 3 minutes at his dad's retirement party. On his card he wrote 'Dad's career'. He spoke for 9 minutes, covered 4 jobs and 2 countries, and ended with 'so, yeah'. You can catch this early: **if your sentence has no verb, it's a topic**. A topic has no end, so your talk won't have one either.

cards.prompt: Your cousin texts you a photo of her index card for tomorrow's 3-minute talk and asks 'is this a destination?' What's the quickest test you text back?

options.text: Can you say it out loud in under 10 seconds, and does it have a verb?
Does it cover everything you plan to say, so nothing gets left out?
Is it short enough to be a slide title?

whyNot.b: That's the whole route, not the destination: a destination leaves most things out on purpose.
whyNot.c: That's a title, not a point: slide titles are usually topics, and a topic has no verb and no end.

cards.reteach: A destination is one sentence, under 15 words, with a verb, that you can say in under 10 seconds. Short alone isn't enough: 'Expenses' is short and goes nowhere. The verb is what makes it a place to arrive.

cards.title: In one breath
cards.body:
**A talk is a walk to one place**, and the place is a single sentence, under 15 words, with a verb, written before anything else. If you can't say it out loud in 10 seconds, you haven't picked where you're going yet.

Tomorrow: what your listeners already know decides what you cut.
cards.simpler:
**A talk is a walk to one place.** That place is a single sentence, under 15 words, with a verb, and you write it before anything else. If you can't say it out loud in 10 seconds, you haven't chosen where you're going yet.

Tomorrow: what your listeners already know decides what you cut.

cards.body: Pick any talk you might give, even a toast. Write its one sentence in your phone's notes app. **Say it out loud** and time it with the stopwatch. Under 10 seconds, under 15 words, has a verb? Keep it.
cards.simpler: Pick any talk you might give one day, even a toast at a party. Write its one sentence in your phone's notes app. **Say it out loud** and time it with the stopwatch. Is it under 10 seconds? Under 15 words? Does it have a verb? If yes to all three, keep it.

chapter.outcomeLine: You can now write the one sentence your talk exists to deliver and say it out loud in under 10 seconds.
